title: Past the basics
issue: Practising often, but still repeating material she already knows.
sourceLabel: Maya persona · targeted feedback and visible progress
question: Does a specific speaking task reveal improvement better than completed exercises?
boundary: Goal setup exists in the prototype. Teacher choice, lessons and progress comparison are proposed.
scenes: Maya finishes another basic exercise, then struggles to explain a work decision in French. Her effort feels disconnected from what she wants to do.
She selects French, her current level and At work. She writes a specific goal: explain a decision and answer follow-up questions.
Maya chooses a teacher whose approach fits. In a one-to-one lesson, she attempts the work scenario and asks for feedback on where she gets stuck.
At a later lesson, she tries a similar scenario and compares it with her earlier attempt. She and her teacher agree what improved and what to practise next.

title: When real speech is too fast
issue: Recognising written words, but losing the meaning in natural conversation.
sourceLabel: Lucas persona · authentic speech, culture and pronunciation
question: Can the learner follow an unfamiliar speaker after practising connected speech?
boundary: Goal and optional resource entry exist. Listening tools and tutoring activities are proposed.
scenes: Lucas follows a written French phrase, but loses it when someone says it naturally. Replaying the same audio leaves him guessing where one word ends.
He chooses Everyday life and describes the listening problem. He can attach a short audio example so the goal starts with a real situation.
Hear the pieces, then the whole
With his chosen teacher, Lucas asks for the phrase slowly, then at a natural pace. He practises hearing connected words and saying the phrase himself.
He tries a new short clip from a different real speaker. He identifies what he understood and brings the remaining difficulty to his next lesson.

title: A lesson that fits this week
issue: Wanting personal support while an unpredictable week makes rigid schedules hard.
sourceLabel: Léa persona · availability and low-pressure support
question: Can learners arrange one useful lesson without feeling locked into a routine?
boundary: Meeting preferences exist. Live availability, booking and between-lesson practice are proposed.
scenes: Léa wants help with French, but work and travel keep changing her week. She postpones looking for a teacher because a fixed routine feels hard to promise.
Overwhelmed · no room for a rigid plan
She selects Online and the days or time of day that might suit her. She can leave preferences undecided; these choices do not book a session.
Léa reviews a teacher’s actual availability and chooses one session that fits. She checks the time and format before confirming, rather than committing to a recurring schedule.
Keep a connection to her goal
After the lesson, she uses a short teacher-provided exercise when it is useful. She chooses when to book again, without a daily quota or streak to maintain.

title: Adapt without starting over
issue: The same useful material needs a different level of challenge for each learner.
sourceLabel: Teacher synthesis · level adaptation and reusable lesson blocks
question: Does adapting a short template reduce preparation while keeping the lesson relevant?
boundary: This teacher-workspace story is proposed. It depicts separate one-to-one sessions, never a group lesson.
scenes: Gilbert has a useful article, but the next beginner needs support and a later learner needs more challenge. Rebuilding both lessons would duplicate his work.
He opens an existing short lesson template and reads the next learner’s goal. He keeps the useful structure instead of building a long course from scratch.
For the beginner, he simplifies vocabulary and adds speaking prompts. He keeps a separate, more demanding version for the other learner and checks each task himself.
Teach from a plan he owns
Before each separate lesson, he previews the learner’s version and makes a final adjustment. The template supports his teaching without prescribing every moment.

title: A no-show needs a clear next step
issue: An absent learner leaves reserved time, follow-up and the session status unresolved.
sourceLabel: Cautions · no-shows, lost time and administrative work
question: Can the teacher resolve an attendance issue with less back-and-forth and clear status?
boundary: Proposed exception flow. Waiting periods, charges, refunds and cancellation rules remain undecided.
scenes: Gilbert is ready for an agreed online lesson, but the learner has not joined. He does not know whether they are late, confused about the time or unable to attend.
He opens the session details, checks the agreed time and sends a short private message. He records the attendance issue without marking the lesson completed.
The learner explains that they missed the session. Gilbert reviews the available next steps and proposes another time; any policy consequences must be clear before action.
Fair · a conversation, not a guess
Once the learner accepts, the replacement session appears as confirmed. The original remains recorded as missed, so his schedule and lesson notes tell the same story.
Resolved · both people know the plan

title: Helpful AI, with a human check
issue: An AI suggestion can save effort but still contain wrong or unsuitable teaching material.
sourceLabel: Teacher synthesis · creative control and review of AI content
question: Can teachers spot and correct unsuitable content before anything reaches a learner?
boundary: Optional AI drafting is proposed. No live model is connected; no accuracy or time-saving result is claimed.
scenes: A draft is not a finished lesson
Gilbert wants a short grammar exercise for one learner. An AI suggestion looks useful at first, but he knows fluent wording can hide an error or the wrong difficulty.
He reads the proposed answers and explanations. One rule is misleading and the vocabulary is too advanced, so he keeps the draft unshared and flags those parts.
Gilbert rewrites the explanation, adjusts the examples and checks the answer key. If the suggestion is not worth repairing, he discards it and uses his own material.
He previews the final exercise and deliberately shares it with the learner. He remains responsible for the lesson and the final feedback.
